sections.html:
Hancock County is the smallest county in West Virginia, a narrow strip of 88 square miles at the top of the Northern Panhandle, with New Cumberland as the seat. Weirton is the largest city, though only part of it lies in Hancock County. Chester sits at the northern tip.

The 2025 population estimate is 27,729, down 4.7 percent from 2020, and the steel mill in Weirton was announced for closure in 2024. The median home is worth $97,800. Owners occupy 72.4 percent of homes and renters fill 27.9 percent of occupied units. The 2020 census counted 14,241 housing units, 10.1 percent of them vacant.

The assessor divides the county into six tax districts: Butler Tracts, Chester, Clay, Grant/Newell, New Cumberland and Weirton. Part of Weirton lies in Brooke County, so if you have a Weirton address, confirm which county's assessor and sheriff bill the parcel.

West Virginia sorts every property into four classes. Class I is currently exempt. Class II is land owned, used and occupied by the owner solely for residential purposes, which includes mobile homes on land the owner does not own, plus farm land.

Everything else is Class III outside a municipality or Class IV inside one. Hancock County's municipalities are Chester, New Cumberland and Weirton. Class III and IV property is taxed at double the Class II rate, and Class IV also bears the municipal levy.

Mobile homes or buildings on land owned by someone else are treated as personal property. Farm land valued for farm use is appraised on fair rental value, which usually produces a lower figure than market value.

The assessor's 2026 levy page shows a Class II total of 1.34826 per $100 of assessed value, in a table that lists no municipal levy.

The bill is the levy rate times assessed value, which is normally 60 percent of market value. The homestead exemption removes $20,000 of assessed value. Pick your district from the dropdown on the assessor's levy page, because the table changes with the district.

Schools received about 69 percent of the 2024 levy. The state report for that year lists $29,138,264 levied on all property in the county: $20,068,364 for schools, $6,435,055 for the county, $2,530,583 for municipalities and $104,262 for the state. A $2,406,368 bond levy sits inside the school figure.

sections.h2: The assessor's office and filing dates
sections.html:
The assessor values property and also collects a few small county fees. The office is at 102 North Court Street in New Cumberland, telephone (304) 564-3311. Fees include $3.00 for a building permit, $2.00 for a mobile home decal, $1.00 per page for a property record printout and $3.00 for a dog license.

  • Personal property returns: every resident reports taxable property owned on July 1, and the return is due between July 1 and October 1. Not filing can complicate vehicle registration renewals.
  • Business personal property: returns are due by October 1, and a business that fails to file forfeits appeal rights.
  • Farm use valuation: first-time applicants file between July 1 and September 1.
  • Homestead exemption: apply between July 1 and December 1 at the assessor's office. An owner who turns 64 on or before the July 1 assessment date should apply so the exemption starts with the next year's taxes.

The assessor's site also offers a property search, sales records, tax maps, map cards and a tax estimator.

Take a disputed value to the county commissioners, who double as the Board of Equalization and Review and open their sessions by February 1. The board can settle a valuation by approving an agreement signed by both the taxpayer and the assessor, so a negotiated result is possible before any formal hearing.

A raise needs five days of written notice to you first, and the board holds assessments to 60 percent of true and actual value at most. Owners who never apply lose that year's correction, though the Office of Tax Appeals remains open. Your evidence has to make your side more likely than not.

Real estate left unpaid may be sold as a lien. The county's Tax Office page carries a heading for a Deputy Land Commissioner's Land Sale. The office is at 102 N. Court Street, with mail to P.O. Box 458, New Cumberland, WV 26047, and an online search is available.

Statewide dates apply: September 1 and March 1 for the two halves, October 1 and April 1 when they go delinquent, and yearly interest of 9 percent. Land still behind on September 1 is listed by the sheriff by September 10. Liens that no one redeems are certified to the State Auditor on October 31.

At closing the seller typically covers the transfer tax while the closing agent clears any open tax ticket. The deed tax is $1.10 on every $500 of value, with a county tax opening at 55 cents and capped at $1.65, and the transfer fee is $20. Only a buyer who agrees to take the deed without it shifts that cost.

Liability for a year's tax rests with the July 1 owner. If you close in the fall, ask your title agent how the second half is being split, and get a payoff from the Tax Office ahead of the September list.

sections.h2: What to bring to the assessor or Tax Office
sections.html: A short trip saves delays. Bring your deed or the paperwork that shows how you came to own the house, your latest tax ticket, and a photo ID. Ask for the district, class and assessed value on file, and for a payoff if anything is open. For a mobile home, bring the title and ask which desk carries it. The assessor's office at 102 North Court Street can also print property records at $1.00 per page.

sections.h2: Selling an older Hancock County home
sections.html:
Sellers here often hold a house that has been in the family for decades, sometimes in one of the river towns, sometimes a mobile home on rented ground. Settle the classification question early. A mobile home on land owned by someone else is personal property, and a house on your own land used as a residence is Class II. Ask the assessor to confirm how yours is carried before you hand records to a buyer.

When back taxes, repairs or an estate hold up a sale, a cash buyer can take the house as-is. The title agent then pays what is owed out of your proceeds.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Hancock County property tax?
faqs.a: The Hancock County Sheriff's Tax Office, 102 N. Court Street in New Cumberland, with mail to P.O. Box 458. Call 304-564-3311, and an online search and payment site is available.

faqs.q: What is the Hancock County property tax rate?
faqs.a: The assessor's 2026 table gives a Class II total of 1.34826 per $100 of assessed value, with Class III and IV at double that. Class IV inside a city adds the municipal levy, so check the levy page for your district.

faqs.q: Is Weirton taxed by Hancock County?
faqs.a: Mostly, but part of Weirton is in Brooke County. Confirm which county's assessor and sheriff bill your parcel before you sell.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Hancock County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Homeowners aged 65 or over, or certified totally and permanently disabled, who have lived in West Virginia two years straight. The benefit is $20,000 off assessed value. File at the assessor between July 1 and December 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hancock County house with delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing pays delinquent taxes and interest out of your proceeds. Contact the Tax Office at 304-564-3311 for a payoff figure before the September list is prepared.
